---
title: "Course outline"
---

This preliminary outline combines mathematical reading,
lectures, and computational laboratories. The pace and selection
of advanced topics may change as the materials develop.

## Part I. Foundations of optimal control

### 1. Controlled dynamical systems

- States, controls, and admissible trajectories.
- Linear systems and the solution formula.
- Exact propagation under piecewise-constant controls.

Laboratory: simulate the integrator and double integrator;
compare analytical and numerical trajectories.

[Lecture 1. Formulation of an Optimal Control Problem](lectures/lecture-01.qmd)

### 2. Reachable sets and controllability

- Fixed-time reachable sets.
- Convex geometry and supporting directions.
- Controllability versus bounded-control reachability.

Laboratory: construct reachable sets, explore their boundaries,
and test target feasibility.

### 3. Minimum-time control

- Earliest arrival at a target.
- Bang-bang controls and switching geometry.
- Analytical reference solutions.

Laboratory: solve the double-integrator minimum-time problem
and compare analytical and numerical results.

### 4. Objectives and numerical optimization

- Minimum time, minimum energy, and tracking.
- Terminal constraints and penalty formulations.
- Discretized controls and numerical optimization.

Laboratory: compare objectives under the same dynamics and
control constraints.

## Part II. From optimal control to differential games

### 5. Adversarial control

- Pursuer and evader objectives.
- Controls, feedback policies, and information patterns.
- Guaranteed outcomes versus optimal outcomes.

### 6. Constructive pursuit methods

- Pontryagin's direct pursuit methods.
- Pshenychnyi and group pursuit.
- Chikrii's resolving-functions approach.
- Sufficient capture conditions and guaranteed-time bounds.

### 7. Positional strategies

- Krasovskii–Subbotin framework.
- Stable bridges and extremal aiming.
- Numerical approximation and strategy realization.

## Part III. Value functions and computation

### 8. Dynamic programming and Hamilton–Jacobi equations

- HJB and HJI formulations.
- Boundary and terminal conditions.
- Verification and nonsmooth value functions.

### 9. Strategy evaluation

- Common benchmark problems.
- Opponent collections and approximate best responses.
- Sensitivity, discretization, and reproducibility.

## Part IV. Learning-based methods

### 10. Learning controllers and value functions

- Supervised approximation of known solutions.
- Closed-loop evaluation.
- Neural value-function approximation.
- Adversarial training and its limitations.

## Prerequisites

The course assumes familiarity with:

- Linear algebra.
- Multivariable calculus.
- Ordinary differential equations.
- Basic Python programming.

Additional mathematical tools will be introduced when needed.

## Reading

The initial reading follows Blagodatskikh and selected material
from Evans. Later topics use specialized differential-games
references.

See the [sources page](sources.qmd) for the developing bibliography.
